mcqs.question: What should determine which columns get indexed on a table, according to the answer skeleton?
options: Every foreign-key column, regardless of whether it's queried
Whichever columns are alphabetically first in the table's schema definition
Every column with a data type that supports indexing, to maximize future flexibility
The columns that appear in the WHERE and ORDER BY clauses of the table's actual frequent queries
mcqs.explanation: Indexes should match real, frequent query filters and sort orders, since that's where they pay off. Indexing every foreign key or indexable column regardless of query usage adds write cost with no guaranteed benefit; alphabetical order is irrelevant to query performance.

mcqs.question: For a query that filters on status equality and sorts by created_at, why does column order in a composite index matter?
options: It doesn't matter — a composite index serves a query identically regardless of column order
The equality-filter column should come first and the sort/range column second, or the query can't use the index as efficiently
The most recently added column to the schema should always be listed first in any index
Column order only matters for indexes with more than five columns
mcqs.explanation: A composite index is effectively sorted by its leading column first; putting the equality-filter column first lets the database narrow down quickly, then use the second column's order for the sort. Reversing that order breaks the efficient match for this specific query shape — order matters even for two-column indexes.

mcqs.question: What cost does every index on a table impose, regardless of how useful it is for reads?
options: It requires the table to be taken offline whenever the index is created
It permanently changes the primary key of the table to include the indexed column
It has to be updated on every insert, update, or delete that touches the table, slowing every write
It prevents the table from ever being sharded across multiple physical nodes
mcqs.explanation: Every index is maintained on every write to the table, so more indexes mean more write-side work regardless of whether any query ever uses them. Index creation doesn't require offline downtime in most systems, doesn't touch the primary key, and doesn't block sharding.

mcqs.question: Why is "index most columns just in case a future query needs it" a pitfall at scale?
options: An unused index is pure write-cost with no read benefit, since no real query ever scans it
Databases enforce a hard limit of two or three indexes per table
Extra indexes make read queries slower even when they aren't used by the planner
It's actually the recommended approach for any table expected to grow significantly
mcqs.explanation: An index nobody queries still gets updated on every write, so it's a permanent cost with zero offsetting read benefit. Databases don't enforce a small fixed index limit, an unused index doesn't slow reads that don't touch it, and this reflexive approach is exactly what the pitfall warns against, not a recommendation.
